newsitem.title: UK: Downpours don't dampen fears of drought in UK.
newsitem.headline: Downpours don't dampen fears of drought in UK.

text.p: Britain has reclaimed its rainy reputation with the wettest June in a century, but experts warned on Tuesday that the rainfall was not enough to quench a country parched by its driest period for two hundred years.

June's rainfall splashed in at 133.7 milimetres across England and Wales, double average levels and the wettest since 1860 when 150 milimetres of rain made that month the soggiest since records began.
Betting chain William Hill has already cut the odds on daily rain in July to 40-1 from 50-1 as the month started with showers in London.

At the Wimbledon tennis championships, Centre Court is showing damage from the covers used to fend off the rain, which disrupted timetables and forced an extra day of play on Sunday June 29 to catch up on matches rained off in the first week.
"I've never seen Centre Court so chopped up," said the top-ranked player Pete Sampras.
In Somerset, south-west England, the annual Glastonbury open air rock festival turned into a mud bath at the weekend and organisers bought 100 tents from Oxfam to provide shelter for fans.

"The statisticians are playing wettest Junes and the British public is getting on with what it is best at: sitting in the rain in a triumph of hope over expectation of a nice day," the Times newspaper said.
But despite the downpours, parts of the country are still parched by a drought caused by the driest period for 200 years, which was only quenched in May.
Around the country there are areas which have bans on water use, with 800,000 customers of Southern Water in Sussex forbidden to use sprinklers on their gardens.
"Despite having just experienced...the wettest June this century, the current drought has not ended," the Environment Agency said.
"The more it rains, the happier we are, but we're still not out of the woods yet," said a spokesman for Thames Water, adding that the company could not rule out introducing curbs on water use.
Groundwater levels are at record lows in many parts of the country and the ground is so dry that it is acting like a giant sponge to soak up the rain, preventing it from reaching rivers.
At the same time, growing plants, trees and crops are slurping up water almost as fast as it falls.
"However much it rains over the summer, reservoirs and groundwater resources will not improve," the Environment Agency warned.
But at least demand from the public is dampened by the rain, with less water used on gardens and other non-essential use.
At the same time, the recent dry weather has made people more aware of the need to conserve water, companies said.
"People have become very receptive to saving water, we've seen a lot of support for our initiatives to cut down use," a spokesman for Southern Water, now owned by Scottish Power, said.
The new centre-left Labour government pushed water supply high up the political agenda just two weeks after it won power in a landslide victory on May 1 by calling a crisis summit on the drought.
It introduced a 10-point plan to tackle drought conditions, including mandatory targets for cutting leaks, which allow nearly 800 million gallons of supplies to seep out of pipes daily.
High levels of leaking, combined with fat executive pay packets, hefty shareholder payouts and poor supplies during the drought have made the water companies deeply unpopular with the public.
Labour has vowed to tax their "excess profits" with a one-off levy which could raise five billion pounds ($8.3 billion) in its first budget, which will be announced on July 2.
Nevertheless, the government's moves and media coverage of environmental damage from the drought have helped to raise public awareness of the need to conserve water.

And companies themselves are trying to improve relations with the public, with many offering free water-saving devices and advice while Thames has also launched a mobile multimedia exhibition to tour its customers.
"Water is at the top of everybody's agenda now, people are used to the idea of a drought," said a spokesman from another water company. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
